clue.text: Sailor carts back pastry seen at the Tate

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor

indicators.note: back tells us the word carts is to be read from its end to its start

parts.note: a tart is a pastry case with a filling

explanation.surface: A sailor wheels carts back and a pastry turns up in the London gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pastry' tempts as the definition, but the Tate, a group of British galleries famous for modern works, points the solver to what is shown there.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-figurative painting and sculpture is exactly the kind of work a visitor finds hanging in the Tate Modern gallery.

clue.text: Makefire water

explanation.surface: An instruction to light a blaze alongside a mention of water.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'Makefire' is 'Make fire' run together. A burn is the Scottish word for a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: To burn is to blaze or set alight, and in Scotland a burn is a small stream or brook of running water.

clue.text: Teased Edward about a relative

indicators.note: about places the word for Edward around the relative, surrounding it

parts.note: Ted is a familiar short form of the name Edward
an aunt is a family relative

explanation.surface: Edward made fun of a family member.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean mocked or provoked someone with jibes.

clue.text: A female who won the Men's Singles in'75

definitions.text: who won the Men's Singles in'75

parts.note: she is the pronoun for a female

explanation.surface: A trivia puzzle asking which woman won the men's tennis title in 1975.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ashe won the Wimbledon men's singles in 1975; 'female' is a pronoun trap, since the winner was a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe, the American tennis player, took the Wimbledon men's title in 1975.

clue.text: Sat back row — it was more to one's liking

indicators.note: back tells us the word sat is read in reverse order

parts.note: taken as written before being turned
a tier is a row of seats, one above another

explanation.surface: Someone sat in the back row of the theatre and enjoyed it more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns SAT into TAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is more flavoursome and palatable suits a person's preference better.

clue.text: Cream, or cream with the top skimmed off

indicators.note: the top of a down word is its first letter, so skimming it off drops the opening C

explanation.surface: A dairy note: cream, or cream that has been skimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: In northern English and Scots dialect the word for cream is the cream word without its C, so both halves give the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots and northern dialect, the dairy top of milk is called by this old word.

clue.text: Fitting way to claim for oneself

explanation.surface: A suitable method of taking something for yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means suitable or proper; as a verb it means to take possession of something, often without permission.

clue.text: Planner with a chequered career

explanation.surface: A designer whose working life has had ups and downs.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'chequered career' usually means a patchy one; here it is a life spent on a chequered board playing draughts, the British name for checkers.
explanation.definitionFit: One who draws technical plans is a drafter, and a player of checkers on its chequered board fits the second reading.

clue.text: Oddly, it could result in firing big guns in the War Office

definitions.text: Oddly, it could result in firing big guns in the War Office

parts.words: Oddly, it could result in firing big guns in the War Office
parts.note: firing means sacking: a policy of laying down weapons could see top brass, the big guns, dismissed from the ministry of war

explanation.surface: A paradox of military policy causing heavy artillery to be fired at the ministry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firing big guns' looks like shooting artillery, but means dismissing important people, which giving up arms might oddly bring about.
explanation.definitionFit: Reducing or abolishing weapons and armed forces would leave senior generals without jobs.

clue.text: Lady with a lamp calls for a hurricane lantern

explanation.surface: A woman holding a lamp asks for a storm lantern.
explanation.walkthrough: Florence Nightingale, the Victorian nurse, was called the Lady with the Lamp. Split the answer as NIGHT IN GALE: a dark, stormy time that calls for a hurricane lantern.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Crimean War nurse carried a lamp on her rounds, and a stormy dark evening needs a storm-proof lantern.

clue.text: Dressed in fine feathers while grinding away

parts.note: to be dressed in clothes is to be wearing them
down is the soft fine plumage of birds

explanation.surface: Someone in their finery is hard at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine feathers' usually means smart clothes; here it is literal plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe gradually eroding something or someone through persistent friction or pressure.

clue.text: Father in physical distress

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A dad finds himself in bodily trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical suffering or hurt is an ache felt in the body.

clue.text: Claim made by a prospector

parts.note: a gold-seeker stakes a claim to dig, and also cries out a possessive word asserting ownership of it

explanation.surface: A gold-digger stakes out a patch of land.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both a cry of ownership and an excavation for ore.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the possessive cry 'that's my property', and also the pit a prospector digs on his claim.

clue.text: Stretched out the arm in pain again

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
to have ached is to have been in pain

explanation.surface: Someone extended their arm and felt it hurt once more.
explanation.definitionFit: Extending a hand towards something is the act of stretching for it.

clue.text: Hell holes for a rich man in hell

explanation.surface: Grim places for a wealthy man in torment.
explanation.walkthrough: Dives is the traditional name of the rich man in the Bible parable of Lazarus, who ends in torment; dives are also seedy bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Seedy bars are called dives, and Dives is the name tradition gives the wealthy man in the parable of Lazarus.

clue.text: Who made the cheater reform?

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the word cheater is remade into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Asking who got the dishonest pupil to mend their ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolmaster or tutor is the person who would correct a pupil who copies in tests.

clue.text: 500 to I favourite all backed was no so hot

indicators.note: all backed says every piece together is read in reverse

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500
a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: A racing tip: the favourite at long odds that everyone backed was a disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all backed' reverses the whole string D-I-PET to give the answer. '500 to 1' and 'favourite' suggest betting, but 500 is just D.
explanation.definitionFit: Lukewarm water or a half-hearted welcome is only mildly warm.

clue.text: Restaurant car patron

explanation.surface: A customer in the dining car of a train.
explanation.definitionFit: A dining car on a train or a roadside eatery is so called, as is anyone eating at a restaurant.

clue.text: The forerunner of a tap dancer's shoe

explanation.surface: The early version of a tap-dancing shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tap' looks like tap dancing; one sense is the water pump used before taps were plumbed in.
explanation.definitionFit: Before indoor plumbing, water was drawn by a hand-worked device, and a light slip-on ballet or dancing slipper shares the name.

clue.text: Furnace for forging link

indicators.note: forging means hammering into a new shape, so the letters of link are reshaped

explanation.surface: A blacksmith's furnace used to make a chain link.
explanation.definitionFit: An oven used for firing pottery or bricks is a type of furnace.

clue.text: Health centre motto should be appropriate

explanation.surface: A gym slogan ought to be suitable.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as BE FIT, an exhortation a gym might adopt.
explanation.definitionFit: A gym would urge its members to get in shape, and to suit or become something is to be proper for it.

clue.text: In the middle of ordering bees for example I invest

indicators.note: ordering puts the letters into a new order, rearranging them

explanation.surface: A beekeeper puts money into the hive while sorting the bees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invest' looks financial, but in military language to invest a town is to surround it.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest a fortress in the old military sense is to surround it with troops and lay siege.

clue.text: Jack takes in military doctors by old public transport

indicators.note: takes in means the sailor word holds the doctors inside it

parts.note: a jack tar, or tar, is a sailor
RAMC is the Royal Army Medical Corps, the British army's doctors

explanation.surface: A sailor carries army medics on an old trolley.
explanation.definitionFit: A street vehicle running on rails, once common in British towns, is an early form of public transport.

clue.text: How chess games are decided by patient people

explanation.surface: Checkmate decides chess, played by calm types.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as IN MATES: games end in checkmate. 'patient' means hospital patients, not calm people.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents of an institution such as a hospital or asylum are its occupants.

clue.text: Hauled along by old copper and teased

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for an old penny, a copper coin
to rag someone is to tease them

explanation.surface: An old policeman was pulled along and mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman; it is a copper coin, the old British penny, written d.
explanation.definitionFit: To be pulled roughly along the ground is to be towed or hauled.

clue.text: Wine put up at camping sites

explanation.surface: Wine on offer at a campsite.
explanation.walkthrough: Tent is an old name for a dark red Spanish wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Tent is a sweet Spanish red wine, and a canvas shelter is what campers pitch.

clue.text: Polynesian food extract from nectar oranges

indicators.note: extract from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A Pacific island dish made from a juice of nectar and oranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A starchy tropical root, staple of Pacific island cooking, eaten as poi in Hawaii.

clue.text: To silence ducks drive them away

parts.note: sh is the sound made to hush someone
a duck is a zero score in cricket, so ducks are two Os

explanation.surface: Hushing the ducks to send them off.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so 'ducks' are the zeros OO.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection used to scare off birds or animals tells them to leave.

clue.text: Swing because a killing was done

explanation.surface: A change of direction because there was a murder.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn or swerve sideways is to swivel, and the old past tense of slay means killed.

clue.text: Miss spring

explanation.surface: Skipping a girl in springtime.
explanation.definitionFit: To omit something is to pass over it, and to leap lightly is to bound.

clue.text: What a hungry wedding photographer should do to surpass all others

definitions.text: What a hungry wedding photographer should do

explanation.surface: Advice to a hungry wedding photographer.
explanation.walkthrough: Literally, a hungry photographer should seize the wedding cake, or photograph it; the idiom means to beat everything.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to be the most outstanding or outrageous, beating all competition.

clue.text: Wake up before prigs managed to tackle the real problem

indicators.note: before puts the waking piece in front of the rest

parts.note: to come to is to regain consciousness

indicators.note: managed means handled or rearranged, so the letters of prigs are reworked

explanation.surface: Getting out of bed before the prudes got to grips with matters.
explanation.definitionFit: To grapple with a difficulty is to face it directly and deal with it.
